# Threads and channels

Some work cannot be made async. Crunching numbers, compressing data, or processing images keeps the
CPU busy from start to finish, so waiting on an event loop does not help. What you need is a second
path of execution that really runs at the same time. Nim provides one through `Thread[T]`,
`createThread`, and `joinThread`, plus `Channel[T]` to send the results back.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can create a thread with `createThread`, wait for it with `joinThread`, send
results through `Channel[T]`, check `compileOption("threads")`, and choose between threads and
`async`.
:::

## A first thread

A procedure that runs on its own thread is marked with the `{.thread.}` pragma. It takes a single
argument value, given at creation time. The result does not come back as a return value; it is sent
through a `Channel` instead.

```{.nim}
import std/typedthreads

var results: Channel[int]

proc square(n: int) {.thread.} =
  results.send(n * n)

proc main() =
  results.open()
  var worker: Thread[int]
  createThread(worker, square, 5)
  worker.joinThread()
  echo results.recv()
  results.close()

main()
```

```{.txt}
25
```

Save it as `main.nim`, then run `nim c -r main.nim`. The module is named `std/typedthreads`; the name
`std/threads` does not exist in Nim 2.2.12. `Thread[int]` means the procedure takes one `int`.
`createThread(worker, square, 5)` runs `square(5)` on a new thread, and `joinThread` waits until that
work is done.

`Channel[int]` is a queue that is safe to use across threads. `send` puts one value in, `recv` takes
out the value that waited longest. Because `joinThread` is called first, `recv` is certain to find
the value that was already sent. `close` releases the channel once it is no longer needed.

A thread procedure takes a single argument. When several values have to travel together, wrap them
in a `tuple`. A procedure with no argument uses `Thread[void]`, as in the next example.

## A `Channel` for a fixed order

The second thread runs at any moment, so printing from inside it makes the output depend on the
scheduler. A `Channel` fixes that: the worker only sends messages, and the main thread prints them
in queue order.

```{.nim}
import std/typedthreads

var messages: Channel[string]

proc produce() {.thread.} =
  for word in ["alpha", "beta", "gamma"]:
    messages.send(word)
  messages.send("done")

proc main() =
  messages.open()
  var worker: Thread[void]
  createThread(worker, produce)
  worker.joinThread()
  while true:
    let message = messages.recv()
    if message == "done":
      break
    echo "got: ", message
  messages.close()

main()
```

```{.txt}
got: alpha
got: beta
got: gamma
```

The `"done"` message is the end marker. Because the queue returns messages in the order they went
in, the output is always `alpha`, then `beta`, then `gamma`. This is how to keep an example
deterministic even with more than one path of execution: do not depend on time, depend on queue
order.

## Typed channels

A `Channel` fixes its type when it is declared, and every message has to match that type. When the
data has several parts, wrap all of them in a `tuple`.

```{.nim}
import std/typedthreads

type Count = tuple[text: string, characters: int]

var results: Channel[Count]

proc count(text: string) {.thread.} =
  results.send((text, text.len))

proc main() =
  results.open()
  var worker: Thread[string]
  createThread(worker, count, "Nim")
  worker.joinThread()
  let (text, characters) = results.recv()
  echo text, " has ", characters, " characters"
  results.close()

main()
```

```{.txt}
Nim has 3 characters
```

`Channel[Count]` only accepts a `tuple[string, int]`. Each thread has its own heap, so a `ref`
object from one thread must not be used in another. Wrapping a result into one value and sending it
through a `Channel` is the safe pattern. Another option is a global variable, as in the first
example.

## `--threads:on` is no longer needed

In Nim 2.x thread support is on by default, together with the `--mm:orc` memory mode. The extra
`--threads:on` pragma is no longer required. To prove it, `system` offers
`compileOption("threads")`.

```{.nim}
import std/typedthreads

echo "threads enabled: ", compileOption("threads")

proc hello() {.thread.} =
  echo "hello from the worker"

proc main() =
  var worker: Thread[void]
  createThread(worker, hello)
  worker.joinThread()
  echo "back on the main thread"

main()
```

```{.txt}
threads enabled: true
hello from the worker
back on the main thread
```

If you really want to turn threads off, use `--threads:off`; then `compileOption("threads")` is
`false`. For this chapter the default is already correct.

## Threads or `async`?

Both run work at the same time, but for different loads.

| Load | Choice |
|---|---|
| waiting on a socket, file, or the network | `async` |
| computing on the CPU without a pause | threads |
| many idle connections | `async` |

The `async` model uses one thread and rotates the tasks that are waiting, so it fits work that is
dominated by waiting. A thread uses another CPU core, so it fits work that is dominated by
computation. Threads are more expensive to create, and memory is not shared for free, so they are
not worth one per tiny task.

Each thread has its own heap, so a `ref` object created in one thread must not be used in another.
When data has to cross a thread boundary, send it through a `Channel` or keep it in a simple global
variable.

One old note: `std/threadpool` with `spawn`, `^`, and `sync` still exists, but it is marked
`deprecated` in Nim 2.2.12. The compiler suggests nimble packages such as `malebolgia`, `taskpools`,
or `weave`. This chapter uses the standard library only, so `Thread` and `Channel` are what it
reaches for.

## Deliberate error: the wrong `Channel` type

A `Channel` checks the type of its messages at compile time. Taking a message as a different type is
rejected before the program runs.

```{.nim}
import std/typedthreads

var channel: Channel[string]

proc produce() {.thread.} =
  channel.send("42")

proc main() =
  channel.open()
  var worker: Thread[void]
  createThread(worker, produce)
  worker.joinThread()
  let n: int = channel.recv()
  echo n + 1
  channel.close()

main()
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(13, 23) Error: type mismatch: got 'string' for 'recv(channel)' but expected 'int'
```

The `type mismatch` message names the type it found and the type it expected. `Channel[string]` can
only hand out a `string`. There are two fixes: change the type of the target variable to `string`,
or change the channel type to `Channel[int]` and send a number from the start.

## Exercises

1. Change the first example so the worker sends two results, then read both with `recv`.
2. Without running it, predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   import std/typedthreads

   var channel: Channel[int]

   proc addOne(a: int) {.thread.} =
     channel.send(a + 1)

   proc main() =
     channel.open()
     var worker: Thread[int]
     createThread(worker, addOne, 41)
     worker.joinThread()
     echo channel.recv()
     channel.close()

   main()
   ```
3. Write from scratch: one thread sends five numbers through a `Channel[int]`, and the main thread
   adds them up while the queue still has messages.
4. When is a thread a better fit than `async`? Name one workload.
5. The code in the error section fails to compile. Fix it by changing the channel type, then explain
   its message.

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- The `{.thread.}` pragma marks a procedure that runs on its own thread.
- `createThread` starts a thread, `joinThread` waits for it to finish.
- `Channel[T]` moves values of one type between threads with a fixed queue order.
- In Nim 2.x threads are on by default; `compileOption("threads")` is `true`.
- Use `async` for work that waits, threads for work that computes.
